paragraphs: The following assessments concern on-site work practices for film, television, and performance lighting technicians; they do not predict hiring, project contracts, or credential outcomes.

Lighting technicians turn program or visual requirements into safe, stable, reproducible lighting effects: setting up fixtures and consoles, wiring and testing, focusing and operating on site, maintaining and dismantling equipment, and completing required records and handovers.

Wholly fictional lighting exercise: given a fictional site plan and equipment list containing 6 fixtures, 1 console, and 1 rigging point, plus two exceptions—an obstructed lighting position and a wiring fault—write a setup sequence, safety points, and testing and fault-handling records within 60 minutes. Do not use real production information or unauthorized materials.

Sample outputs and reflection: check whether structural load capacity and power are verified first, whether equipment is grouped by central control and circuit, and whether testing and exception records are retained. Then consider whether you can stay focused during pressured rehearsals, work at height under safety procedures, and accept responsibility for equipment and site safety.

Lighting technicians install, maintain, and dismantle fixtures, lighting controls, and related lighting electrical and rigging equipment for photography, television, film, video, and live performances. They may focus or operate fixtures or fit gels and accessories. This page covers O*NET 27-4015.00, excluding related roles such as electricians, electrical and electronics engineering technicians, and robotics technicians.

entries: Work inputs: fixtures and accessories, lighting consoles and dimming or circuit systems, power and signal cables, rigging and structures, filming or performance sites and program requirements, and venue and safety conditions.

Verifiable outputs: lighting positions and console layouts meeting requirements, reproducible effects and testing records, safety and securing inspection records, maintenance and fault-handling records, and dismantling and return inventories.

Complete workflow: survey site structures and power → set up fixtures and rigging to requirements → wire, patch, and test → focus and operate on site → inspect and respond during filming or performances → dismantle, count, and return equipment afterward → record maintenance and exceptions.

paragraphs: Key judgments: confirm effects with the lighting director and verify structures, rigging, and power with personnel who have the required competence and authorization. Stop affected work and report defects. Occupational task descriptions do not authorize structural load approval, electrical work, or work at height.

Work may involve moving, setting up, and operating equipment in studios, theaters, or outdoor locations. The broader BLS equipment technician group describes nights, weekends, and deadline pressure. O*NET provides only partial data for this occupation and does not establish the hours, noise, or frequency of work at height claimed on this page; verify conditions for each project.

Tools and materials: fixtures, gels and diffusion accessories, lighting consoles and dimming circuits, cables and connectors, rigging and securing equipment such as stands, trusses, and scaffolds, color charts and light meters, CAD, project management and spreadsheet software, and basic repair tools.

Collaboration chain: lighting directors and operators; cinematography, directing, and production teams; stage, venue, and rigging crews; electricians and venue safety managers; equipment rental and maintenance staff. Report exceptions and changes beyond scope through the established process.

Quality standards: lighting positions and effects meet requirements, testing is reproducible, wiring and rigging are safe and reliable, fixture condition is traceable, dismantling and inventories are complete, and exceptions are reported promptly.

Lighting technicians may perform lighting wiring and minor repairs within their training and authorization. This does not grant authority over fixed power systems, structural approvals, or related electrical or engineering roles. Electricians and technicians have overlapping work objects; verify boundaries by the actual work and local rules rather than excluding all electrical tasks based on job titles.

Electrical and electronics engineering technicians help design, test, and support electrical or electronic systems and usually do not set up lighting positions or operate performance lighting on site. Lighting technicians focus on on-site setup, testing, and operation of fixtures and lighting control systems.

Robotics technicians maintain and test robotic systems and automation equipment. Lighting technicians work with entertainment lighting equipment and consoles, with different work objects and safety standards.

Electricians handle fixed electrical installations and power compliance. Lighting technicians perform temporary lighting power connections, wiring, and testing within authorization; they do not replace electrician qualifications.

Plumbers and solar photovoltaic installers work with piping, water and gas systems, and photovoltaic power systems, respectively. Lighting technicians handle entertainment lighting equipment and rigging and do not take on work across equipment categories.

In projections for the broader broadcast, lighting, and sound systems occupational group, BLS mentions that technology and AI may reduce the staffing needed for setup and operation. This is a projection mechanism, not causal research showing layoffs among lighting technicians, and it provides no organizational adoption rate.

Before setup, appropriate personnel verify power, structures, and rigging; during testing, check consoles and circuits. Operate according to equipment and project emergency procedures; cutting all power is not a safe response to every exception.
First use a wholly fictional plan and fixture list for a reversible offline rehearsal. Record judgments and review results; do not let unverified automation prompts replace on-site checks.

U.S. Lighting Technician Pay and Employment Scope

U.S. 27-4015: May 2025 median annual pay of 68,060 USD and median hourly pay of 32.72. The exact BLS 2025—2035 row shows employment falling from 9,900 to 9,400, a decline of 4.8% (rounded to -5% in OOH), a net loss of about 500, and 600 average annual openings. O*NET still displays old 2024 projections; do not splice them together. The original online percentile table beyond the median was not reobtained in this round.

OEWS employee wages exclude self-employment income. BLS reports a 12.2% self-employment share in 2025 employment for this exact occupation, which does not support saying that most are freelancers. Verify project contract fees, duration, and net income after costs separately.

Wage percentiles describe distribution positions, not pay bands for newcomers, experienced workers, touring crews, or union productions. Beyond the median, the original percentile table was not reobtained in this round. Retained values await independent verification and cannot establish causes of income differences.

The current O*NET page lists 2024 employment shares of 25% in information and 24% in arts, entertainment, and recreation, without breaking down the remaining 51%. These are older-period shares. The four industry wages in BLS OOH belong to the broader 27-4010 group and cannot be used as 27-4015 lighting wages.

BLS reports about 9,900 employed in 2025 for this exact occupation; the O*NET profile contains only partial data. Label the period and scope of wages, employment, and industry information separately. Do not present the broader group's 136,600 workers or 9,800 average annual openings as this occupation's figures.
Fit Signals: Start with Observable Work Behaviors

To assess fit, first consider whether you can stay focused under deadline and rehearsal pressure, work at height and run cables under safety procedures, collaborate with cinematography, directing, and stage teams, and accept equipment and site safety responsibilities. RIASEC and similar tools can only suggest hypotheses; they cannot replace actual task experience.

Positive signals: strong practical skills, quick understanding of lighting positions and effect requirements, acceptance of irregular hours and touring travel, and patience and recordkeeping habits during repeated testing.

Conditions requiring caution: difficulty with overtime or reversed day and night schedules, discomfort with height and electrical risks, limited adaptability to on-site changes, or difficulty staying steady during pressured communication.

Trial action: use a wholly fictional site plan and fixture list to write a setup sequence, console and circuit assignments, responses to two exceptions, and testing records. Ask someone else to verify using the records.

Current O*NET occupational interest scores are R100 and C52, with RC as the top two categories. Work-style information includes dependability, attention to detail, and caution. None is a personal assessment score or safety qualification.

General personality measures such as the Big Five provide no job-specific evidence for this occupation and support self-reflection only. Continue checking through actual setup, testing, and collaboration exercises.
Type tools such as MBTI and the Enneagram cannot determine competence or safety qualifications; use them for self-reflection only.

Entry Paths and Capability Stages

For this exact occupation, BLS lists typical U.S. entry preparation as a postsecondary nondegree award, related experience of None, and short-term on-the-job training. OOH explains that specific roles range from high school to college requirements. O*NET Job Zone 3 describes general preparation, not uniform education, years of experience, or legal permission.

Verify U.S. job education, training, and electrical work rules separately. In China, check whether the actual work falls under the special operations catalog; where applicable, workers must complete specialized training and assessment and obtain an operator certificate before starting. The title lighting technician does not establish a nationwide absence of qualification requirements.

Training records, manufacturer certifications, and job authority are different statuses. Certification does not automatically authorize work at height, electrical work, or venue management. Stop work beyond qualifications and authorization and transfer it to an authorized party.

Begin with paper plans, inventories, and offline console practice. Before actual wiring, work at height, or rigging, verify work qualifications, training, supervision, and project authorization; supervision does not automatically waive certification requirements.
Evidence to show: use a verifiable lighting position and console plan, testing records, and safety checklist to demonstrate procedural response and collaboration skills.
Next step: check the target project's console, fixture, and safety training requirements, then verify setup, testing, and operating skills in a supervised production crew.

Prepare for programming, effect design, training, or technical management. Appointment and structural or power approvals require additional competence and authorization; tenure does not automatically expand the legally permitted work scope.
Market Signals and Transition Directions

BLS exact occupation 27-4015: 9,900 employed in 2025 and about 9,400 in 2035, down 4.8%, a net loss of about 500, and 600 average annual openings. Do not mix these with O*NET's old 2024—2034 projections or the broader 27-4010 group.

The current O*NET page still lists 2024 industry shares of 25% in information and 24% in arts, entertainment, and recreation, with only partial occupational data. Label BLS projections separately as 2025—2035. Explain projections, industry structure, and specific project opportunities separately.

Transferable skills: fixture and console operation, wiring and safety protection, on-site testing and operation, collaboration with production and cinematography teams, and equipment maintenance and recordkeeping.

Skills to add: experience with the target project's console and fixture models, safety training or certification, or the tools and rules needed to move into electrical work, stage technology, or performance management.

career_risk_cards.heading: Lighting Technicians: Work Risks and Boundaries

risks.consequence: Falls, falling-object injuries, or dropped fixtures.
risks.mitigation: Check structures and load capacity before setup, use compliant rigging and protection, and stop and escalate when conditions are inadequate.
risks.scenario: When work at height or rigging is improperly secured.

risks.consequence: Electric shock, short circuits, or fire.
risks.mitigation: Stop affected work if capacity, wiring, energy state, or personnel qualifications are unverified, and refer it to personnel meeting applicable rules for procedural handling. This page provides no wiring instructions.
risks.scenario: When temporary power, cable sizing, or grounding is improper.

risks.mitigation: Maintain cooling and safe clearances, secure equipment firmly, and inspect temperature and condition.
risks.scenario: When fixtures overheat, are obstructed, or equipment becomes unstable.

risks.consequence: Electric shock, fire, or equipment faults.
risks.mitigation: Stop minor repairs beyond competence and authorization and report to the supervisor. Electrical isolation, verification, and repairs must be handled procedurally by personnel meeting applicable rules.
risks.scenario: When minor repairs expand into power modifications or dismantling begins before the energy state is established.

risks.affected_roles: Programming, setup, and on-site operation roles
risks.consequence: Mismatched effects or operations and unreviewed safety conditions.
risks.mitigation: The responsible person confirms changes and synchronizes versions; appropriate personnel recheck affected safety conditions before work resumes.
risks.scenario: When lighting positions or circuits change just before rehearsal or performance and the version is not shared with control and setup personnel.

risks.consequence: Lighting positions, load capacities, or circuits do not match the actual site.
risks.mitigation: Verify against actual on-site structures and power, and retain review and escalation records.
risks.scenario: When visualization or system prompts are assumed usable without on-site verification.
risks.title: Uncritical acceptance of automation or visualization prompts

description.text: Lighting technicians turn program and visual requirements into safe, stable, reproducible lighting effects for film, television, video, and live performances: setting up fixtures and consoles, wiring and testing, focusing and operating on site, maintaining and dismantling equipment. Work is often project-based or freelance and involves work at height, wiring, and deadline pressure. When evaluating this career, examine the complete workflow, responsibility boundaries, evidence definitions, risk controls, and observable entry-level work samples together.

title.text: Evaluating a Career as a Lighting Technician: Work, Entry, and Risk Boundaries

subject.name: Lighting Technicians
subject.summary: Lighting technicians install, test, operate, and dismantle fixtures, lighting controls, and related lighting electrical and rigging equipment for photography, television, film, video, and live performances. They may focus or operate fixtures or fit gels and accessories. Work is organized by project or production crew, often freelance or on short-term contracts, with responsibility for equipment and site safety.
